profile.summary: 1 Samuel narrates Israel's transition from a tribal, fragile confederation threatened by external enemies and within undisunion itself to a centralized monarchy. The book shows that the search for a king was not, in itself, a break with God's plan, but the way in which the Lord led history under his sovereignty. Saul is presented as the first king, chosen and even favored by God, but his disobedience disqualifies him. In contrast, David is separated to reign and proceeds to represent the lineage by which God will fulfill his saving purpose. The work emphasizes that human leadership is insufficient unfeasure to the covenant, and that God preserves his people even in the midst of the failure of his leaders.
profile.setting: The backdrop is the period of the judges, when the tribes of Israel lacked unity and faced military and spiritual pressure. The source points out that the Mosaic law itself already provided for Israel's possibility to ask for a king, while at the same time warning against the typical excesses of human royalty and demanded that the king meditate on the law of God. The book comes at this moment of national crisis, in which the people want a ruler who unites the tribes and offers security. As for composition, there is uncertainty: tradition associates the name of the book with Samuel's central role, but the final editor is unknown. It is also recognized that Samuel originally circulated as a single work and that its final form may have been achieved after the use of various sources and possibly near the time of Solomon or after exile. The preserved text presents relevant handwritten variants in some excerpts, although few change the general sense.

structure.label: Samuel: Birth, Formation and Early Leadership
structure.description: Birth of Samuel, his dedication to service in the tabernacle, his call as a prophet and his role as a judge who calls on Israel to repentance and fidelity before the Philistine oppression.

structure.label: Demand for a King and the Anointing of Saul
structure.description: Israel asks for a king like the other nations; Samuel warns the people, but the Lord guides Saul's choice and anointing as the first king.

structure.label: Confirmation of the reign and farewell of Samuel
structure.description: Saul gets an initial victory over the Ammonites and Samuel makes his farewell speech, reminding the people of God's faithfulness and calling him to the fear of the Lord.

structure.label: Saul's disobedience and his rejection
structure.description: Saul reveals his infidelity in decisive deeds; Samuel confronts him, and the Lord rejects him as king by his disobedience.

structure.label: David's choice and the conflict between Saul and David
structure.description: Samuel anoints David in secret; David gains prominence, Saul comes to see him as a threat and attempts to eliminate him, while divine providence prevents his plans against David from succeeding.

structure.label: The Final Persecution and the Death of Saul
structure.description: Saul's opposition continues to the tragic outcome: Saul and Jonathan die in the battle against the Philistines, paving the way for David's ascension.

themes: The sovereignty of God over the history of Israel
The Inadequacy of Human Leadership Without Obeth to the Covenant
The role of the prophet as an interpreter and guardian of the word of God
The tension between the monarchy desired by the people and the divine standard for the king
Preparation of the Davidic Lineage and Redeeming Range of Divine Promise
readingKeys: Notice how the passage of the leadership of the judges to the monarchy is not narrated as simple political advance, but as God's response to a spiritual and national crisis.
Read Samuel's speeches carefully, as they interpret the events and make clear the divine criterion for evaluating kings and people.
Compare the deeds of Saul and David: the source wants to show contrast between disobedience and faithfulness, between the rejected king and the king chosen by God.
profile.cautions: The introduction does not for sure fix authorship or the final date of composition; Samuel's name in the title is due more to its historical importance than to the full authorship. There are also textual differences between ancient handwritten traditions, although, according to the source, most do not significantly change the meaning of the book.

dossier.narratedEra: Main setting in the period of the judges, in the transition to the unified monarchy in Israel: time of Samuel, Saul and the beginning of David's accession. The notes place the narrative with the tabernacle in Shiloh, the Philistines as a constant threat and the passage of a tribal federation to a centralized kingdom.
dossier.compositionEra: The final composition of 1 Samuel is presented as unidentified author/editor's work. The notes recognize the possibility that Samuel wrote part of the material of his own time, with continuity by prophets linked to David, but also record the academic proposal of a final essay during or after Babylonian exile (586-538 BC), with a final possibility already close to the reign of Solomon (971-931 BC). The Hebrew tradition and the Septuagint treat the work differently as to the title and division, but the book was originally part of a single work with 2 Samuel.

politics.title: From the tribal confederation to the centralized monarchy
politics.detail: The book is read as a record of Israel's transition from a federation of tribes to a centralized kingdom, motivated by internal and external threats and the desire of a king to unify the nation.
politics.readingImpact: It helps to read the request by king not only as a political whim, but as a response to a crisis of national cohesion and security; at the same time, the narrative criticizes excessive trust in human structures.

politics.title: The monarchy under restrictions of God's law
politics.detail: The notes link the royal ideal to Deuteronomy 17:14-20: the king should be chosen by God, not multiply horses, women and wealth, and should continually study the law.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of Saul and after other kings must be done in the light of a theological pattern prior to the kingdom: the problem is not the existence of monarchy itself, but its submission or not to the covenant.

politics.title: Samuel as prophetic authority over the king
politics.detail: Samuel appears as a prophet-judge with authority to anoint kings and also to rebuke them when they go beyond the limits of the covenant, as in 1M. 13:8-15 and 15:10-33.
politics.readingImpact: The text does not present the king as the supreme instance; prophetic criticism continues above the throne, which shapes the whole reading of Saul and David.

politics.title: Philistines and the vulnerability of Israel
politics.detail: The notes treat the Philistines as hostile and recurring power, with military advantage especially in flat terrain and ability to impose humiliation by defeating kings and troops.
politics.readingImpact: The battles of 1 Samuel are not only military episodes; they reveal the fragility of Israel and the need for faithful leadership and the sovereign action of God.

politics.title: Saul, Jabesh-gilead and the dispute with Ammon
politics.detail: Saul's initial victory over the Ammonites and the ransom of Jabesh-gilead in 1Sm 11 are highlighted as part of the initial legitimization of his reign.
politics.readingImpact: Saul's reign begins with a concrete saving act, which intensifies the tragedy of his subsequent disobedience and fall.

customs.title: Annual pilgrimage and cult in the central sanctuary
customs.detail: Elkanah rises annually to the place of worship because the law required participation in three annual feasts and the sacrifice in the sanctuary chosen by God; the tabernacle is in Shiloh at this stage.
customs.readingImpact: The family piety of 1Sm gains weight: the text presupposes regular practice, not private devotion isolated, and situates the narrative in a concrete religious center.

customs.title: Sacrifices with community meal
customs.detail: The notes note that certain sacrifices included portions of meat consumed in a community meal.
customs.readingImpact: The scene of the cult in Shiloh is not only sacrificial; it involves table, coexistence and family tensions, which helps to explain Anna's domestic conflict.

customs.title: Polygamy and domestic rivalry
customs.detail: The text highlights that simultaneous marriage to two women normally produced serious friction, as in the case of Elcana with Ana and Penina.
customs.readingImpact: Ana's pain and the conflict of the home are not peripheral; the family structure itself already carries tension, which deepens the reading of her suffering and prayer.

customs.title: Voting of Ana and consecration Nazirey
customs.detail: Anna's vow is understood as a promise to return the child to the Lord as a Nazirite; the note suggests even the expectation of a new type of liberator similar to Samson.
customs.readingImpact: Samuel is introduced from birth as a separate person to God, which gives meaning to his future public function in worship and leadership.

customs.title: Purification before the sacrifice and the environment of Shiloh
customs.detail: Before David's sacrifice and anointing, there is mention of personal purification, including bathing and sexual abstinence. In Shiloh, the cultual environment could be morally confusing, to the point that Eli suspected Anne was drunk.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the holiness of worship lives with human disorder; this prepares criticism of the priesthood and corrupt religious life.

customs.title: Military life and squire functions
customs.detail: The squire appears as the chief warrior's personal assistant; David has already occupied this function, and the enemy's corpse could be stripped of goods as a sack of war.
customs.readingImpact: The scenes of 1Sm 16 and 31 gain social concretion: the war includes personal hierarchies, humiliation of the loser and search for spoils.

language.title: Lord of the Armies and language of divine war
language.detail: The note explains that the title "Lord of the Armies" may refer to the heavenly hosts, human armies or foreign armies used by God, and anticipates the theme of God as a warrior in 1M.
language.readingImpact: Anna's prayer and the narrative of the ark are not only devotional; they place God as a military sovereign above the forces of the valley and the neighboring peoples.

language.title: "House/Tree of the Lord" for the tabernacle
language.detail: The notes clarify that the wording "the temple of the Lord" in 1M. 1:9 is literal in Hebrew, but refers to the tabernacle, since Solomon's temple did not yet exist.
language.readingImpact: He avoids anachronism and shows that Samuel's central cult takes place in a portable sanctuary, not in the temple of Jerusalem.

language.title: "Filha de Belial" as an expression of moral contempt
language.detail: The expression translated as "impartial woman" is explained as "beail of Belial," that is, someone marked by uselessness or perversity.
language.readingImpact: The language reinforces the shock of the unjust accusation to Ana and shows how the moral vocabulary of the text is strong and classification.

language.title: The Heart as Divine Criterion of Choice
language.detail: In 1 Sam 16, the note insists that God looks at the heart, not the appearance or height; this contrasts with Saul and Eliab, both of which are impressive outwardly.
language.readingImpact: The reader is instructed to interpret David's choice as theological, not aesthetic and social.

language.title: The anointing and the presence of the Spirit
language.detail: The notes highlight that the Spirit of the Lord came powerfully upon Saul and then upon David, but left Saul because of disobedience.
language.readingImpact: The narrative of 1 Samuel is read as a history of the presence and withdrawal of divine empowerment, not only as a political succession.

language.title: Literary parallels with Jz 9 and Saul's death
language.detail: Saul's death is compared to that of Abimelech in Judges 9, reinforcing the pattern of failed kings and shameful outcome.
language.readingImpact: Saul's end is not an isolated accident; he echoes the kind of degenerate leadership that the book of Judges had already shown.

timeline.title: Time of judges and national disintegration
timeline.detail: The introduction places 1 Samuel in the decline of the judges' period, culminating in the chaos of Judges 17-21 and in the search for national unity.
timeline.readingImpact: 1 Samuel is read as a narrative and theological response to a previous crisis, not as an isolated beginning of Israel's history.

timeline.title: The generation of Gideon, about a century before Samuel
timeline.detail: The notes say that Gideon lived about a hundred years before Samuel and acted similarly to a king by accumulating gold, having many women, and naming a son, and amyelche.
timeline.readingImpact: The story of 1 Samuel is set in continuity with previous monarchical tendencies, showing that the problem does not begin with Saul.

timeline.title: Silo as a culture center in Samuel's day
timeline.detail: The tabernacle was in Shiloh from the days of Joshua to the age of Samuel.
timeline.readingImpact: Samuel's childhood and the beginning of the book should be read in a central cult setting prior to the temple of Jerusalem.

timeline.title: The capture of the ark and the absence of Samuel
timeline.detail: The notes note that Samuel apparently had no national prominence when the Philistines oppressed Israel and captured the ark; he is absent from 1 Sam 4:1-7:2.
timeline.readingImpact: This prevents the reader from force Samuel into all the scenes: the narrative highlights his gradual ascent, not a continuous performance from the beginning.

timeline.title: First real anointing and rejection of Saul
timeline.detail: Samuel anoints Saul in 1 Sam. 10:1 and then David in 16:13; and then Saul is rejected by his unfaithfulness in 1 Sam 13 and 15.
timeline.readingImpact: The temporal sequence shows that royalty in Israel undergoes concession, testing and substitution; the plot is governed by fidelity to the covenant.

timeline.title: Fall of Saul and open way to David
timeline.detail: The death of Saul and Jonathan in 1Sm 31 prepares the ascension of David, even though with later difficulties already in 2 Sam 1:1-5:5, mentioned only as continuity of history.
timeline.readingImpact: The end of 1 Samuel functions as a historical turn: the rejected king falls and the anointed heir awaits the moment of reigning.

investigation: The traditional authorship is treated with caution: Samuel may have written part of 1 Samuel, but the final editor is not identified.
There is debate about the composition: some scholars defend multiple sources and post-exile writing; the note also admits a final form already close to Solomon's reign.
Samuel originally formed a single work; the division into two books comes from the Septuagint and after the Hebrew tradition.
The manuscript notes recall that the Greek tradition, the Gaugetic Hebrew tradition and Qumran manuscripts diverge at various points, although most variants do not significantly alter the meaning.
The cover is selective: the material provided especially emphasizes 1Sm 1, 8-17 and 31, in addition to the introductory frame; other parts of the book appear only in summary mode.

Some historical connections are presented as inference or theological reading, not as independent proof; this is worth, for example, for the proximity between Judges' events and 1 Samuel and for the relationship between deuteronomic texts and the monarchy.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the notes provided and therefore reflects a partial coverage of 1 Samuel. The sources focus on the general introduction and selected excerpts (especially 1, 16 and 31), leaving without treatment many episodes and social details of the book. Where the notes advance historical or compositional hypotheses, they were maintained as proposals of secondary source, without increasing this the independent historical certainty. There are also real controversies about dating, authorship and literary unity; the dossier distinguishes them, but does not resolve the debate. Finally, some aspects of the historical-cultural context appear only when the notes mention them directly; no gaps were filled with external reconstructions.
